```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  dev = if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) "ragg_png" else "png")
```

Character mode redraws a ggplot on a grid of monospaced characters, the way
home computers of the 1980s drew charts on a text screen. The grid prints as
text in the console, and `char_figure()` turns it back into a ggplot of glyphs
that can be saved as a figure, in black and white or in the colors of a
Commodore 64 screen.

```{r packages}
library(ggplot2)
library(inferplotR)
```

## A plot on a text grid

`char_grid()` takes a single-panel Cartesian ggplot, builds it and draws its
layers into a character matrix. The output is deterministic: the same plot
and arguments always give the same grid.

```{r grid, comment = ""}
chicks <- aggregate(weight ~ Time, data = ChickWeight, FUN = mean)
p <- ggplot(chicks, aes(Time, weight)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Chick weight", x = "Days since birth", y = "Mean weight (g)")

char_grid(p, width = 56, height = 16)
```

From the top, the grid holds the title, the y-axis label, the plot rows, the x
axis with a `+` at every break, the tick labels, the x-axis label, the legend
and the caption. The first series draws lines with slope glyphs chosen for
cells twice as tall as wide.

Supported layers are rectangles (bars, columns, tiles), ribbons and areas,
smooths (the line only), paths and lines, segments, error bars and ranges,
reference lines, points and text. Other layers, such as box plots and violins,
are skipped with one warning of class `inferplotR_skipped_layer`. Facets and
flipped, polar or transformed coordinates are errors of class
`inferplotR_unsupported`.

### Several series

Series are told apart by glyph, never by color. The key comes from the first
discrete scale among `fill`, `colour`, `shape` and `linetype` with at least two
breaks, and the legend under the grid shows each series' glyph:

```{r series, comment = ""}
diets <- aggregate(weight ~ Diet + Time, data = ChickWeight, FUN = mean,
                   subset = Diet %in% c("1", "4"))
q <- ggplot(diets, aes(Time, weight, linetype = Diet)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Days since birth", y = "Mean weight (g)", linetype = "Diet")

char_grid(q, width = 56, height = 14)
```

## Character sets and case

`charset = "unicode"` uses box-drawing glyphs for lines, geometric shapes for
points and block glyphs for fills; `"ascii"` (the default) stays within
printable ASCII. `case = "upper"` writes every string in upper case, as on
machines without lower-case letters; the glyphs of the data do not change.

```{r unicode, comment = ""}
tooth <- aggregate(len ~ dose, data = ToothGrowth, FUN = mean)
bars <- ggplot(tooth, aes(factor(dose), len)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Dose (mg/day)", y = "Mean tooth length (mm)")

char_grid(bars, width = 40, height = 12, charset = "unicode", case = "upper")
```

A grid prints with `print()`; `format()` and `as.character()` return its lines,
and the object also holds the character matrix (`chars`) and the legend table.

```{r lines}
g <- char_grid(p, width = 56, height = 16)
dim(g$chars)
nchar(as.character(g))[1:3]
```

## A grid as a figure

`char_figure()` draws a grid as a ggplot made only of text, one glyph per
non-blank cell. The `"bw"` style is black on white without a margin, the 1-bit
style of the package, with a 64 x 20 grid by default.

```{r bw, fig.width = 5.3, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "The chick weight chart drawn as black monospaced characters on white: asterisks and slope glyphs for the line, plus signs on the axes."}
char_figure(p)
```

The `"c64"` style imitates the screen of a Commodore 64 after power-on: light
blue glyphs on a blue screen inside a light blue border, a 40 x 25 grid, labels
in upper case and, by default, `READY.` with a cursor below the chart. The two
colors are the VIC-II "blue" (`#352879`) and "light blue" (`#6C5EB5`) of the
Pepto palette by Philip Timmermann. They are the only colors in the package.

```{r c64, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "The chick weight chart in upper case on a blue screen with a light blue border, ending with READY. and a cursor, like a Commodore 64."}
char_figure(p, style = "c64")
```

## Sizing and saving

Glyphs only line up if the figure is saved at the size of the grid.
`char_size()` computes it: the grid fills `width_mm` (134 mm, the Bleisatz text
width, by default), each cell is `width_mm / ncol` wide and `cell_ratio` times as
tall, and the c64 border adds 8 % of `width_mm` on every side.

```{r size}
char_size(p)
char_size(p, style = "c64")
char_size(p, width_mm = 86)
```

Pass the size to `save_figure()`, and the same `width_mm`, `cell_ratio` and
`style` to `char_figure()` and `char_size()`:

```{r save}
fig <- char_figure(p, width_mm = 86)
size <- char_size(fig, width_mm = 86)
out <- save_figure(fig, file.path(tempdir(), "chicks-char.png"),
                   width = size$width, height = size$height, dpi = 300)
file.exists(out)
```

The text size is chosen so that one glyph advance fills one cell:
`(width_mm / ncol) / char_width` mm, where `char_width` is the advance width of
the font in em. The default 0.6 fits IBM Plex Mono and DejaVu Sans Mono.

## The C64 font

The figures above use `figure_font("mono")`: IBM Plex Mono when it is installed,
otherwise R's generic `"mono"` family. For the look of the real machine, install
the C64 Pro Mono font by Style64. Its license does not allow it to be bundled, so
it is not part of this package. Make it known to the graphics device (for
example through systemfonts for the ragg devices), then use square cells one em
wide:

```{r c64-font, eval = FALSE}
c64 <- char_figure(p, style = "c64", family = "C64 Pro Mono",
                   char_width = 1, cell_ratio = 1)
size <- char_size(c64, style = "c64", cell_ratio = 1)
save_figure(c64, "chicks-c64.png", width = size$width, height = size$height)
```

## Sources

The C64 colors are the Pepto palette of the VIC-II chip by Philip Timmermann,
as shipped with the VICE emulator in `pepto-pal.vpl`. IBM Plex is released
under the SIL Open Font License (<https://github.com/IBM/plex>). See the README
for the full list of sources.
